claims.claim: The Speculiction reviewer says these flash-forward throwaway lines are fewer in Sailing to Sarantium than in A Song for Arbonne and all but dry up once Crispin reaches Sarantium.
claims.quote: by the time Crispin arrives in Sarantium they all but dry up
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'Forever utilizing the patient voice'

claims.feature: other: two moons and cosmetic markers
claims.claim: Palmatier calls devices such as two moons or a changed landscape mere cosmetic changes, and locates Kay's craft in subtler alterations.
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'How he does is it arcane'

claims.claim: Palmatier says that for him the true art of Kay's work is not in the use of language but in the subtle skewing of a familiar setting.
claims.quote: is not in the use of language

claims.feature: other: flash-forward over a whole life
claims.claim: Capossere describes a quick in-and-out flash forward tied to a character the narration has just been close to, telling in one sentence what that character would remember all his life.
claims.quote: a simple, quick in and out flash forward

claims.claim: Capossere writes that Written on the Dark is not a seamless narrative but more a series of situations, pausing on a time and then jumping ahead over intervening months or years.
claims.quote: not a seamless narrative but more a series of situations

claims.claim: Capossere names as a major theme the way small decisions by people overlooked by the history books - tavern poets, bartenders, guardsmen - can have major impact.
claims.quote: the tavern poets, the bartenders, the guardsmen

claims.claim: lepusdomesticus objects that Tigana invents species names - trialla and grele in place of nightingales and partridges - and calls them smeerps.
lepusdomesticus argues that invented names for endemic species are distracting rather than verisimilitude-increasing, because a fantasy world will not mesh with accepted reality anyway.
lepusdomesticus says the invented species names in Tigana feel completely arbitrary because they appear to have no bearing on the plot or the rest of the story.

claims.feature: other: prologue as a false beginning
claims.claim: lepusdomesticus argues that both the Prologue and Chapter One of Tigana are false beginnings that name many characters who never reappear.
claims.quote: Chapter One of the novel are false beginnings

claims.claim: The Quill to Live book club reports that half the group scored Tigana nine or above and the other half scored it below five, for an average of a solid seven.
claims.source: Andrew, 'Book Club Discussion: Tigana By Guy Gavriel Kay', The Quill to Live, 17 March 2016
claims.quote: half of the group had scores of nine or above

claims.claim: Erfael says Kay works in a style where everything that happens is somehow important or represented, which can come across as contrived.
claims.quote: everything that happens is somehow important or represented

claims.claim: The thread's opening poster says Tigana is almost written like a play, being long conversations of pure dialogue with little else.
claims.quote: The book is almost written like a play.

claims.claim: The forum member chokipokilo says Kay uses flashbacks and internal monologues a great deal and that the way he blends history into the narrative amazes him.
claims.quote: The way he blends history into the narrative

claims.claim: chokipokilo says the coincidental revelation is a device Kay uses in all his works and that after a few books a reader starts to see it coming.
claims.quote: that's a device GGK uses in all his works

verdicts.trueWording: Thankfully, however, there are not as many A Song for Arbonne, and by the time Crispin arrives in Sarantium they all but dry up.
verdicts.note: Raw live page (blogspot, HTTP 200). Quote exact. The preceding sentence supplies both other limbs: 'there are numerous throwaway lines to the effect "Later, he, too, would have cause to be privately grateful..."' (the proleptic aside) and 'there are not as many A Song for Arbonne' (fewer than in Arbonne). Byline 'Jesse', dated Tuesday, May 6, 2014, in the paragraph beginning 'Forever utilizing the patient voice of the storyteller'.

verdicts.trueWording: such as having two moons or changing the landscape, but these are mere cosmetic changes. Kay's craft is much more subtle.
verdicts.note: Live tor.com returned HTTP 403; recovered via Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20181116160422id_/https://www.tor.com/2016/07/06/altering-the-familiar-tigana-by-guy-gavriel-kay/ (raw HTML, not a summarizer). Quote exact. Both limbs supported in one sentence, and the next sentence locates the craft in subtler alteration. Byline Joshua Palmatier, 'Wed Jul 6, 2016 12:30pm', paragraph beginning 'How he does is it arcane in and of itself'.

verdicts.trueWording: But for me, the true art of Kay's work is not in the use of language, but in the subtle way he skews what is so obviously a familiar setting.
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture. Quote exact. 'for him' = 'for me'; the skewing-of-a-familiar-setting limb is the same sentence's second half. It is the final body paragraph, immediately before the author bio, as the claim states.

verdicts.trueWording: Sometimes it remains tied to a character we've just been in tight with, a simple, quick in and out flash forward.
verdicts.note: Live fantasyliterature.com returned HTTP 403; recovered via Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20250624011037id_/https://fantasyliterature.com/reviews/written-on-the-dark/ (raw HTML). Quote exact. The 'character the narration has just been close to' limb is verbatim in the same sentence; the one-sentence-whole-life limb is the block quote that follows: 'All his life, and he lived a very long time, and even saw Sarantium again, Gauvard Colle would remember that afternoon, that room.' Review by Bill Capossere, dated May 20th, 2025.

verdicts.trueWording: The story, therefore, is not a seamless narrative but more a series of situations.
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture. Quote exact. The pausing/jumping limb is the immediately preceding clause: 'the way it pauses for a while to focus on a time, then jumps ahead to detail another period, skipping over whatever intervening months/years took place.'

verdicts.trueWording: small decisions can have major impact... by those often overlooked by the history books: the tavern poets, the bartenders, the guardsmen.
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture. Quote exact, in the paragraph opening 'Thematically, Kay brings in a number of subjects. A major one...' — so 'major theme' is supported. The page's sentence is broader than the claim (it also covers decisions by 'kings and queens and other "greats"'), but the claim asserts nothing the page does not; it is narrower, not contrary.

verdicts.trueWording: Here be smeerps! We have trialla and grele instead of nightingales and partridges.
verdicts.note: Raw live page (LiveJournal, HTTP 200). Quote exact. All limbs present in one sentence, in the section headed 'WORLD-BUILDING'. Post titled 'Tigana: Head Smashing', by lepusdomesticus, dated March 31 2014; the author is addressed as 'Susie' in the post's own text. The page notes grele is actually from Chapter 2.

verdicts.trueWording: in practice it is distracting, since a fantasy world by its very nature will not mesh with the rules of accepted Reality, so no amount of this kind of invention will actually increase its verisimilitude
verdicts.note: Same raw live page. Quote exact. Both limbs — distracting rather than verisimilitude-increasing, and the not-meshing-with-accepted-Reality reason — are in the same sentence, in section 'WORLD-BUILDING'. Its subject is 'endemic species' names.

verdicts.trueWording: where it seems that these changes will have no bearing on the plot or the rest of the story... it feels completely arbitrary
verdicts.note: Same raw live page, same sentence as index 503 (section 'WORLD-BUILDING'). Quote exact, and the causal 'because... no bearing on the plot or the rest of the story' limb is the page's own subordinate clause.

verdicts.trueWording: Indeed, both the Prologue and Chapter One of the novel are false beginnings... we are introduced by name to a lot of characters who are never going to show up again
verdicts.note: Same raw live page, in the section headed 'PROLOGUES'. Quote exact. Both limbs supported. Minor nuance recorded, not deducted: the page hedges the never-reappearing limb with a bracketed spoiler, '[Spoiler! Until a couple of them turn out to be Not Really Dead After All!]', and the claim's 'many characters' = the page's 'a lot of characters'.

verdicts.trueWording: half of the group had scores of nine or above and the other half of the group had scores below 5... average for the group was a solid seven
verdicts.note: Raw live page (HTTP 200). Quote exact, in the opening paragraph. All three limbs — nine-or-above half, below-five half, 'a solid seven' average — are in consecutive sentences. Post by Andrew (Andrew Mather), March 17, 2016; the page also gives 'Bookclub - 7.0/10'.

verdicts.trueWording: Kay works in a very epic style where everything that happens is somehow important or represented. This can come across as contrived.
verdicts.note: Raw live page (HTTP 200, full thread rendered without login). Quote exact. Both limbs are consecutive sentences. Post #5 by Erfael, Dec 6, 2011, as attributed. The page qualifies the contrived limb with 'if you're looking for more traditional fantasy storytelling'.

verdicts.trueWording: The book is almost written like a play. It's almost all long conversation of pure dialogue after another with little of anything else.
verdicts.note: Same raw live page. Quote exact including the full stop. Both limbs are consecutive sentences. Post #1 by taoofjord, the thread starter, Dec 5, 2011 — 'thread's opening poster' confirmed by the 'Thread starter taoofjord / Start date Dec 5, 2011' header.

verdicts.trueWording: He also tends to use flashbacks and internal monologues a lot... The way he blends history into the narrative sometimes flat out amazes me.
verdicts.note: Same raw live page, post #6 by chokipokilo, Dec 6, 2011. Quote exact. Claim's 'a great deal' = page's 'a lot'; claim's 'amazes him' = page's 'sometimes flat out amazes me'. Both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: As far as coincidental revelations, that's a device GGK uses in all his works. After reading a few you'll start to see it coming ahead of time.
verdicts.note: Same raw live page, same post #6 by chokipokilo, Dec 6, 2011. Quote exact (page renders a curly apostrophe in "that's"). Both limbs are consecutive sentences; 'after a few books a reader starts to see it coming' = 'After reading a few you'll start to see it coming ahead of time.'
